metadata.note: The lesson names no assigned reading. Reading questions rest on documents the lesson cites and quotes (Meiklejohn et al., the Bitcoin.org developer guide on transactions, the P2P network and the block chain, Biryukov et al., ethereum.org on gas and fees), and each states a fact that is on a visible slide. Only the visible slides count; the hidden slides get no questions. Coverage: one question for each visible check, worked, practice, answers and review slide, and the part slides on change, confirmations, the node checks, the mempool, the coinbase, the explorer and the Ethereum payment.

lectures.title: Blockchain at a Glance - lesson synthesis
Blockchain at a Glance - reading synthesis

questions.question_stem: A case note reads: "Subject received 5,000 USDT on 3 November." What must the analyst establish before searching for that payment?
questions.correct_answer: Which chain the USDT sits on, because the same token is issued on several chains, each its own record.
incorrect_answers: Which explorer the agent prefers, because every explorer shows one shared USDT record for all the chains.
Which wallet the subject used, because the wallet decides which chain's record holds the payment.
Which exchange issued the USDT, because a token from one issuer is recorded only on Ethereum's chain.
questions.explanation: USDT names an asset, not a record. The same token sits on several chains, each a separate record with its own explorer, so the analyst needs the chain first (or the address, whose format shows the chain). Searching the wrong chain finds nothing, and the analyst might report that nothing happened.
questions.lesson_block: Check: a note says "USDT". Where do you look?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Check: a note says "USDT". Where do you look?

questions.question_stem: A Bitcoin payment spends one 0.2 BTC input and creates outputs of 0.05 BTC and 0.1495 BTC. What was the fee, and where is it written?
questions.correct_answer: 0.0005 BTC, written nowhere: it is the input minus the outputs, and a transaction has no fee field.
incorrect_answers: 0.0005 BTC, in the transaction's fee field, which a node fills in when it relays the payment.
0.1495 BTC, written in the change output, because change is the amount the miner keeps as the fee.
0.05 BTC, the smaller output, because Bitcoin always treats the first output as the miner's fee.
questions.explanation: 0.2 - 0.05 - 0.1495 = 0.0005 BTC. A Bitcoin transaction has no fee field: the fee is whatever the inputs hold that the outputs do not pay out, and an explorer shows it only because it looked up the inputs and subtracted. The same holds for a fee of zero.
questions.lesson_block: Check: Alice's fee. Where is it written?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Check: Alice's fee. Where is it written?

questions.question_stem: An analyst reads a Bitcoin payment in block 900,010 while the latest block is 900,012. The agent asks whether it is paid and whether it is final. What does the analyst report?
questions.correct_answer: Three confirmations: paid, being in a block, but Bitcoin never declares a payment final.
incorrect_answers: Three confirmations: paid and final, because every payment in a block is settled for good.
Two confirmations: paid, but not final, because the block it sits in does not count as one.
Three confirmations: unpaid, because no payment counts as paid until it is also declared final.
questions.explanation: Confirmations = 900,012 - 900,010 + 1 = 3, because the payment's own block counts. It is paid because it is in a block, not waiting in a mempool. Final is a different question: Bitcoin never declares a payment final, and each block on top makes reversal harder.
questions.lesson_block: Check: Alice's payment, 3 blocks deep. Final?
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Check: Alice's payment, 3 blocks deep. Final?

questions.question_stem: An analyst opens block 3 in an explorer and reads its parent hash. Which hash is it?
questions.correct_answer: Block 2's hash, the link that joins each block to the one directly before it.
incorrect_answers: The hash of the miner's coinbase, which records who was paid for the whole block.
The hash of block 3's first payment, which is how an explorer finds the transaction.
The hash of block 4, which an explorer adds once another block is mined on top.
questions.explanation: Each block's header holds the hash of the block before it, so the parent hash on block 3's page is block 2's hash. That link is what makes the blocks a chain, and why an edit to an old block breaks every later link.
questions.lesson_block: Worked: find a payment, click by click
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Worked: find a payment, click by click

questions.question_stem: A Bitcoin payment spends one 50 BTC coin and creates two outputs, 10 BTC and 40 BTC. The 40 BTC output pays the same key that received the 50 BTC coin. Which output is change, and how can the analyst tell?
questions.correct_answer: The 40 BTC output: it pays back to the key that owned the coin being spent, as change does.
incorrect_answers: The 10 BTC output, because change is always the smaller of the two outputs in any Bitcoin payment.
Neither: the 50 BTC coin was spent whole, so no change exists until a later payment.
The 40 BTC output, because change is always the larger of the two outputs in any payment.
questions.explanation: Where change goes back to the payer, it is easy to spot: the 40 BTC output pays the key that received the coin being spent. Size is no rule, and the whole 50 BTC coin was spent, with 40 BTC returned as change.
questions.lesson_block: Practice: read block 170's inputs, outputs, fee
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Practice: read block 170's inputs, outputs, fee

questions.question_stem: A Bitcoin payment spends one 50 BTC coin and pays out 10 BTC and 40 BTC. An agent asks for the fee. What is the answer?
questions.correct_answer: Zero: 50 minus 10 minus 40 leaves nothing, and no line of a transaction states a fee, even a zero one.
incorrect_answers: Unknown, because the transaction has no fee field, so only a miner's records show what was paid.
Zero, because the fee field is empty and a payment with an empty fee field is sent free of charge.
10 BTC, the first output, because the amount sent to the payee is what the miner takes as its fee.
questions.explanation: 50 - 10 - 40 = 0 BTC, so the fee was zero. A fee is never written: it is the inputs minus the outputs, whether it is 0.0005 BTC or nothing. In 2009 a miner would take a payment with no fee.
questions.lesson_block: Answers: block 170's payment, field by field
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Answers: block 170's payment, field by field

questions.question_stem: A prosecutor says Bitcoin cannot be hacked, so a reported theft of bitcoin cannot be real. How should the analyst answer?
questions.correct_answer: The hash links make old blocks resist editing, but thefts happen at wallets and exchanges.
incorrect_answers: Editing an old block is easy, so a thief can rewrite the record and take coins back from a wallet.
Wallets and exchanges sit on the chain itself, so thefts happen by editing a block's hash links.
The cryptography is weak, so an attacker can rewrite old blocks and nodes accept the edited copy.
questions.explanation: Edit block 277,316 and every later link breaks, so the record resists change. The cryptography is strong; thefts happen at the endpoints, where keys are held: wallets and exchanges.
questions.lesson_block: Review: four beliefs, and what breaks each
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Review: four beliefs, and what breaks each

questions.question_stem: Alice's wallet holds one unspent 0.1 BTC output, and she pays 0.015 BTC to a cafe. What does the chain record for the coin she spent?
questions.correct_answer: The 0.1 BTC output is spent whole; two new outputs exist: 0.015 BTC to the cafe, change to Alice.
incorrect_answers: Her balance falls by 0.015 BTC, and the rest of the 0.1 BTC stays in the same output just as before.
The output is debited 0.015 BTC, and the chain keeps a running balance for her address too.
Only 0.015 BTC is spent, and the remainder becomes a new output that her wallet creates later.
questions.explanation: Bitcoin keeps no balances. An unspent output is spent whole, once, so Alice's 0.1 BTC coin is gone and two new coins exist: 0.015 BTC to the cafe and the change, less the fee, back to Alice.
questions.lesson_block: Bitcoin keeps no balances, only unspent coins
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Bitcoin keeps no balances, only unspent coins

questions.question_stem: A person has signed a Bitcoin payment in their wallet but has not sent it. What can an analyst watching the network or the chain see?
questions.correct_answer: Nothing: the signed payment is still in the wallet, and the network sees it only after broadcast.
incorrect_answers: An unconfirmed payment in node memory pools, since signing is what releases a payment to the network.
The block and its time, since signing is what writes a payment into a block on the chain.
The first node to relay it, a weak clue, since signing starts the relay to a node's peers.
questions.explanation: Signing happens in the wallet, so before broadcast there is nothing on the network, and before a block there is nothing on the chain.
questions.lesson_block: Every payment takes the same five steps
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Every payment takes the same five steps

questions.question_stem: A node receives a signed Bitcoin payment whose outputs add up to more than its inputs. What does the node do?
questions.correct_answer: It rejects the payment and does not relay it, since outputs may not add up to more than inputs.
incorrect_answers: It relays the payment on, and the extra amount becomes the fee that a miner collects afterwards.
It holds the payment in its mempool until a miner decides whether the outputs are covered.
It relays the payment on, and the sender's wallet is charged the difference when it is mined.
questions.explanation: Each node checks the signature, that the coin is still unspent, and that the outputs do not add up to more than the inputs. A payment that fails stops at the first honest node.
questions.lesson_block: Nodes check a payment before passing it on
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Nodes check a payment before passing it on

questions.question_stem: An explorer shows a Bitcoin payment as "Unconfirmed". What may the analyst report about it?
questions.correct_answer: The explorer's node has seen it waiting in the mempool; it is not settled and can still vanish.
incorrect_answers: The payment is made, but the explorer has not yet counted its confirmations, so it is settled.
The nodes rejected the payment, since a valid payment is never left unconfirmed by nodes.
The payment is in a block, but the block is too new for the explorer to show its time yet.
questions.explanation: "Unconfirmed" means seen, not settled. The payment waits in the nodes' memory pool, and one never mined tends to fade as peers restart. An analyst who reports it as made can be wrong.
questions.lesson_block: Unconfirmed is not paid: it can still vanish
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Unconfirmed is not paid: it can still vanish

questions.question_stem: A block's first transaction, the coinbase, pays the miner 25.2 BTC when the block subsidy is 25 BTC. Where does the extra 0.2 BTC come from?
questions.correct_answer: The fees paid by the transactions in that block, which the miner collects as well.
incorrect_answers: A second subsidy that the rules add whenever a block holds a great many payments at once.
A tip the network sends to the miner whose block is mined first, on top of the subsidy.
Coins taken back from the previous block's miner when that block's reward is revised.
questions.explanation: The coinbase is the miner paying itself the subsidy plus the fees of every transaction in the block. Alice's 0.0005 BTC fee, for example, is part of her block's coinbase.
questions.lesson_block: A miner packs waiting payments into a block
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: A miner packs waiting payments into a block

questions.question_stem: An explorer page for a Bitcoin address shows the tag "Exchange" beside it. How should the analyst treat the tag?
questions.correct_answer: As a lead of Low confidence: the tag is the explorer operator's claim, not data from the chain.
incorrect_answers: As chain data, because the tag is stored in the transaction with the outputs and amounts.
As High confidence, because an explorer reads its tags straight from the node's own record of the chain.
As worked out by the explorer from earlier transactions, in the same way that it works out the fee.
questions.explanation: On the page, txid, outputs and block come from the chain; input amounts and the fee are worked out from earlier transactions; a tag comes from whoever runs the explorer. A tag alone rates Low confidence: a lead, not a fact.
questions.lesson_block: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras

questions.question_stem: On an account chain such as Ethereum, Account 1 sends 1.5 ETH to Account 2. What does the chain record?
questions.correct_answer: Both balances change, Account 1's down and Account 2's up, and no change output is made.
incorrect_answers: A change output returns the unspent remainder to Account 1, in the same way as on Bitcoin.
Account 1's coin is spent whole, and two new outputs are created, one for each account.
Only the fee moves, since an account chain keeps no balances and records no values.
questions.explanation: Ethereum keeps a balance and a nonce for every account, so a transfer changes two balances. There are no coins to break, so Bitcoin's change clues do not carry over.
questions.lesson_block: One Ethereum payment: nonce, value and fee
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: One Ethereum payment: nonce, value and fee

questions.question_stem: An agent treats every Bitcoin address in a case as one person. Which finding from Meiklejohn and colleagues, who transacted with services themselves, undercuts that?
questions.correct_answer: One person can hold many addresses, and one service's address can hold the money of many people.
incorrect_answers: One address always belongs to one person, but a person can be tied to it only through a court.
Addresses carry the owner's name in the transaction, but explorers remove it before showing it.
A service gives each customer one address, so the address count equals the customer count.
questions.explanation: The lesson cites Meiklejohn et al. for this belief's correction: the chain shows keys and addresses, never people. Many addresses can belong to one person, and a service's address can pool many customers' money.
questions.lesson_block: Review: four beliefs, and what breaks each
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Review: four beliefs, and what breaks each
questions.specific_source_reading: Meiklejohn et al., A Fistful of Bitcoins: many addresses per person and pooled service addresses, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: An analyst asks a Bitcoin node for a payment with getrawtransaction and finds no fee in the answer. Why?
questions.correct_answer: The input names a coin by txid and output number, not by amount, so the fee must be worked out.
incorrect_answers: The node strips the fee before replying, because fees are private and only miners may read them.
Fees are written in the block header, not the transaction, so a node's reply for it never has them.
The fee field is filled in by the miner at mining time, so an unmined payment has an empty field.
questions.explanation: The Bitcoin.org developer guide says an input names the output it spends by txid and output number, not amount. The input's value, and so the fee, must be looked up in the earlier transaction, which an explorer does for you.
questions.lesson_block: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: An explorer is a node's record, plus extras
questions.specific_source_reading: Bitcoin.org developer guide, Transactions: an input names its coin by txid and output number, not amount, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: A node restarts while it holds waiting Bitcoin payments that no miner has included. According to the Bitcoin developer guide, what happens to them?
questions.correct_answer: Its memory pool is lost, so a payment never mined tends to slowly disappear as peers restart.
incorrect_answers: They are written into a block by the restarting node, so they confirm once it is online.
They are written into the next block by the node, because a restart turns it into a miner.
They are marked confirmed after the restart, because a restarting node treats them as settled.
questions.explanation: The developer guide says a peer's memory pool is lost when it shuts down, and a transaction that is never mined tends to slowly disappear from the network as peers restart.
questions.lesson_block: Unconfirmed is not paid: it can still vanish
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Unconfirmed is not paid: it can still vanish
questions.specific_source_reading: Bitcoin.org developer guide, P2P Network: "When a peer shuts down, its memory pool is lost", as the slide quotes it

questions.question_stem: Researchers linked Bitcoin transactions to IP addresses by watching which nodes relayed each one first. How much weight does that evidence carry on its own?
questions.correct_answer: Low confidence, because many wallets use another's node, so the first relay may not be the sender.
incorrect_answers: High confidence, because the first node to relay a payment is always the sender's own node.
Moderate confidence, because a payment cannot be relayed until the sender's own node has checked it.
No weight at all, because nodes relay payments only after a miner has included them in a block.
questions.explanation: Biryukov and colleagues linked transactions to IP addresses this way, but many wallets use another person's node, so the first relay may not be the sender. Alone, that is Low confidence.
questions.lesson_block: Nodes check a payment before passing it on
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: Nodes check a payment before passing it on
questions.specific_source_reading: Biryukov, Khovratovich and Pustogarov: first-relay linkage to IP addresses, Low confidence alone, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: A plain ETH transfer uses 21,000 gas at a gas price of 2 Gwei. What is the fee?
questions.correct_answer: 0.000042 ETH: gas used times gas price is 42,000 Gwei, and a Gwei is a billionth of an ETH.
incorrect_answers: 0.042 ETH: gas used times price is 42,000 Gwei, and a Gwei is a millionth of an ETH.
0.000000002 ETH: the 2 Gwei price is the whole fee, and a Gwei is a billionth of an ETH.
0.000021 ETH: the gas used is the whole fee, counted in Gwei, with no price to multiply.
questions.explanation: Fee = gas used x gas price: 21,000 x 2 Gwei = 42,000 Gwei, and a Gwei is a billionth of an ETH, so 0.000042 ETH.
questions.lesson_block: One Ethereum payment: nonce, value and fee
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: One Ethereum payment: nonce, value and fee
questions.specific_source_reading: ethereum.org, Gas and fees: fee = gas used x gas price; a Gwei is a billionth of an ETH, as the slide states it

questions.question_stem: Someone edits a transaction in an old block of a blockchain. According to the Bitcoin developer guide, what happens?
questions.correct_answer: The block's hash changes, every later link breaks, and nodes reject the edited copy.
incorrect_answers: The block's hash stays the same, so later links hold, and nodes accept the edited copy.
Only that block is rejected, while later blocks still link to it and stay valid.
The edit spreads into later blocks, whose hashes change too, and nodes accept the chain.
questions.explanation: Each header holds the previous block's hash, so editing an old block changes its hash and breaks every later link. Nodes reject the edited copy.
questions.lesson_block: A blockchain is blocks, each linked to the last
questions.specific_source_lesson: 02-IN-blockchain_at_a_glance.qmd: A blockchain is blocks, each linked to the last
questions.specific_source_reading: Bitcoin.org developer guide, Block chain: each header holds the previous header's hash; an edit breaks later links, as the slide states it
